foreground.title: The data behind the search for MH370
foreground.subtitle:
The Australian Government led search operations for the missing Boeing
777 aircraft operating Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 in the southern Indian
Ocean. The search involved the collection and analysis of large volumes of
marine data from a remote area. The data obtained during the first phase of
sea floor mapping is now available to the public.

On 8 March 2014, Malaysia Airlines flight MH370 disappeared from air traffic control radar during a flight from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia to Beijing, China with 239 passengers and crew on board.

After the aircraft transmitted its final automated position report and made an unscheduled change in direction, radar tracked the aircraft crossing the Malaysian peninsula until it was outside of radar coverage range in the Malacca Strait. Based on contact the aircraft had with a satellite ground station, it was discovered that MH370 continued to fly for approximately six hours after it flew beyond the range of radar.
Important features are highlighted and coloured in the text to identify the matching features in the interactive maps.
Explore the interactive maps by double-clicking or using the buttons to zoom in and out, drag and move the map, and select the dots for more information.
The available data indicates the aircraft entered the sea close to a long, narrow arc in the southern Indian Ocean, the 7th Arc.

The initial surface and air search focused on the areas on either side of the Malaysian peninsula, in the South China Sea and the Andaman Sea. Satellite communications data analysis, however, led to the search being shifted to the southern Indian Ocean, where it was coordinated by the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA). From 18 March to 29 April 2014, this search scanned 4.7 million square kilometres of ocean and involved 21 aircraft that conducted 345 individual flights over 3177 hours, as well as 19 ships from eight nations.
A search for the aircraft’s flight recorders was also undertaken at this point. An autonomous underwater vehicle was deployed to scour over 850 square kilometres of sea floor.
Please refer to the Australian Maritime Safety Authority website for information about the timeline of events during the initial weeks of the search.
The search area was determined based on the analysis of probable flight paths and their intersection with the 7th Arc.
Explore the interactive maps by double-clicking or using the buttons to zoom in and out, drag and move the map, and select features for more information.
On 31 March 2014, the Malaysian and Australian governments agreed that Australia would take the lead in the search operation in the southern Indian Ocean.

On behalf of Australia, the then Prime Minister, the Hon Tony Abbott MP, established the Joint Agency Coordination Centre (JACC) to coordinate the Australian Government's support for the search into missing flight MH370.
In May 2014, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) assumed responsibility for conducting underwater search operations for MH370.

Geoscience Australia provided advice to the ATSB on the procurement, technology and planning requirements for the bathymetric survey, and continued to provide expertise and support through the survey and underwater search.

In January 2017, the governments of Malaysia, Australia and the People’s Republic of China jointly announced the suspension of the search for MH370 after the missing aircraft was not located within the 120,000 square kilometre underwater search area. The search has been suspended until further credible evidence is available that identifies the specific location of the aircraft.

The underwater search for MH370 was undertaken in a remote part of the southern Indian Ocean, approximately 2000 kilometres from Perth, which meant it took search vessels up to six days to reach the search area.

image.altText: Distance of the search area from Perth

text.value: The search comprised two phases, Phase One, a bathymetric survey, provided a detailed map of the sea floor topography in the search area; this was used to guide Phase Two, the underwater search. The underwater search used sidescan and multibeam sonar equipment mounted on towed and autonomous underwater vehicles to collect high resolution maps of the sea floor.

The search for MH370 collected 278,000 square kilometres of bathymetry data within the search area and 710,000 square kilometres of data in total, which includes the data acquired in transit between port and the search area. It is one of the largest marine surveys ever conducted.
In addition to the scale of the search area, its remote location makes this bathymetric survey unique.

text.value: In general, the world's deep oceans have had little investigation. Only 10 to 15 per cent of the ocean has been mapped with the sonar technology similar to that used in the search for MH370.
Previous maps of the sea floor in the search area were derived from satellite data, which only showed the depth of the ocean at low resolution.
Continue scrolling to compare previously available data with the data acquired in the search for MH370.
The Phase One data provided maps that are at least 15 times higher resolution than the maps that were previously available.
Continue scrolling to see 3D data of the sea floor around Broken Ridge, comparing data available before and after the search.
A vertical exaggeration has been applied to enhance the 3D effect.
This newly acquired data is the first high resolution data available for these areas; the search area is now among the most thoroughly mapped regions of the deep ocean on the planet.
Explore the interactive maps by double-clicking or using the buttons to zoom in and out, and drag to move the map.

The data has revealed features on the sea floor that were not visible in the previous satellite imagery. This remote area of the Indian Ocean has a variety of sea floor features, including vast seamounts 1500 metres high and kilometres wide, deep canyons and underwater landslides of sediment that travel for kilometres along the sea floor.
Select each dot to view a short video. For a larger view, select the "Full screen" option in the player.

Phase One of the search also acquired backscatter data. Backscatter data measures the strength of the return sonar signal and is used to distinguish between different types of sea floor, such as hard rock and soft sediment. This data was used to identify anomalies on the sea floor to be investigated further during the underwater search.
The major geological feature of the sea floor in the MH370 search area is Broken Ridge. It is approximately 1200 kilometres long and was created by tectonic forces more than 40 million years ago.
While scientists already knew of the existence of Broken Ridge, the detailed bathymetry data shows distinct geological provinces north and south of Broken Ridge for the first time.

The sea floor north of Broken Ridge is more than 40 million years old, making it the oldest sea floor in the search area. The sea floor in this region is covered in a layer of sediment of up to 300 metres thick and is subject to extensive sea floor landslides, some of which are kilometres long. The Gulden Draak Seamount and the Batavia Seamount found in this part of the search area are significant due to their size.
Broken Ridge and the Diamantina Escarpment are a geological ‘breakup zone’, created approximately 40 million years ago as their tectonic plate broke apart.

The sea floor south of the Diamantina Escarpment has the youngest geology within the search area. This region of the sea floor was formed by ‘sea floor spreading’ caused by tectonic plate movements. As a result, the sea floor is highly complex, including a series of ridges, volcanoes, and valleys. The Geelvinck Fracture Zone was the result of the same tectonic motion that created Broken Ridge. It is 900 metres deep and 12 kilometres wide.

While the data was collected for the sole purpose of locating the missing aircraft, it will be of interest to the scientific community as it is some of the first high resolution data of this area of the sea floor.

In addition to the geological insights, the new data will be valuable to scientists across diverse disciplines. The data will help to identify unique sea floor features, which is important for oceanographic and habitat modelling. This data builds on the existing knowledge base of ocean floor processes which will support other areas of future research, including climate and tsunami modelling.

Phase Two of the search collected more than 120,000 square kilometres of high resolution data using sidescan and multibeam sonar mounted on towed and autonomous underwater vehicles. During the search, points of interest were identified and investigated in more detail. An underwater vehicle descended to each of these locations where higher resolution sonar, photographic or video imagery was acquired in order to identify the features.

Sidescan sonar data measures the strength of the returned signal of high-frequency sound pulses that are bounced off the seafloor. This data is used to create a much higher resolution image of the seabed than data acquired during Phase One.
Explore the interactive maps by double-clicking or using the buttons to zoom in and out, and drag to move the map.

As sidescan sonar data has a resolution of less than one metre, it can detect smaller features on the seabed and identify areas that differ from the surrounding environment. These differences can be natural (geological) or artificial features.
During the search, contacts identified by sidescan sonar were divided into three classifications:
• Classification three were of some interest but were of low probability of being significant to the search,
• Classification two were of more interest but were still unlikely to be significant to the search, and
• Classification one were of high interest and warranted further investigation.
Explore the interactive maps by double-clicking or using the buttons to zoom in and out, drag and move the map, and select the dots for more information.
Please refer to the Australian Transport  Safety Bureau website for information about Sonar contact classification during the search.
The investigations located a number of shipwrecks within the search area.
Select each dot to view an image of that underwater feature. There are multiple images for each dot; use the arrow to toggle between them.
A number of other small items were also identified on the sea floor, including whale bones and cable from a vessel.
These findings during Phase Two of the search highlight the level of detail to which the sea floor has been searched.
Select each dot to view an image of that underwater feature. There are multiple images for each dot; use the arrow to toggle between them.

So far more than 20 items of debris have been brought to the attention of the Malaysian investigation team. Items thought to be from MH370 were found along the east and south coast of Africa, the east coast of Madagascar and the Islands of Mauritius, Reunion and Rodrigues in the Indian Ocean. Some were confirmed as definitely coming from the missing aircraft, others were assessed as very likely to be from MH370.
More information on the debris is available from the Malaysian Ministry of Transport.
Select each dot to view an image of that underwater feature. Select the image for an enlarged view.

Using the locations of confirmed debris, the Australian Government’s Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation, the CSIRO, conducted drift modelling analysis to determine possible locations of the MH370 crash site. The results of this modelling were consistent with the search area.

"Despite every effort using the best science available, cutting edge technology, as well as modelling and advice from highly skilled professionals who are the best in their field, unfortunately, the search has not been able to locate the aircraft."
"Accordingly, the underwater search for MH370 has been suspended."
"We remain hopeful that new information will come to light and that at some point in the future the aircraft will be located."
— MH370 Tripartite Joint Communiqué, January 2017

We acknowledge the very significant contribution of Fugro Survey Pty Ltd who acquired additional bathymetry data while the search vessels transited to and from the search area at no cost to the search. This data along with the bathymetry data gathered in the search area is now being released to the public.
Further information on the search for MH370 can be accessed from the JACC or the ATSB.
For more information on the MH370 data release visit the Frequently Asked Questions page on the Geoscience Australia website.
